explain.say: See Bounces off ball lighting up? Light from the Sun or a lamp hits the ball, and some of it bounces off, like a ball bouncing off a wall. That bounced light travels towards your eyes. In the dark, there is no light to bounce. Does that make sense?

explain.say: Now look inside a real eye. See the iris and pupil glowing? The iris is the coloured part, and the pupil is the black hole in the middle where light goes in. In the dark your pupil grows big to let in more light. What colour is your iris?

explain.say: Here is the retina, at the back of the eye. The lens bends the light so a tiny, sharp picture lands on the retina, like a picture on a screen. Strangely, the picture is upside down! Can you guess who turns it the right way up?

explain.say: Your brain! See it light up at the end of the chain. The optic nerve sends the picture to your brain, which flips it and tells you: that is a ball. Brilliant seeing! Wow fact: light is so fast it could zoom around the whole Earth more than seven times in one second.

faq.q: How do our eyes see things?
faq.a: Light from a source, like the Sun, bounces off things and into our eyes. The lens makes a picture on the retina at the back, and the optic nerve sends it to the brain, which works out what we are looking at.

faq.q: Why can we not see in the dark?
faq.a: We see things only when light bounces off them into our eyes. In total darkness there is no light to bounce, so nothing reaches our eyes.
asks: Why do we need light to see?

faq.a: The pupil is the black hole in the middle of the iris that lets light into the eye. It grows bigger in dim light and smaller in bright light.
asks: Why do pupils get bigger in the dark?

faq.q: Is the picture in our eye really upside down?
faq.a: Yes. The lens makes an upside-down picture on the retina. The brain learns to understand it the right way up, so we never notice.
asks: Why do we not see things upside down?

faq.a: The retina is a thin layer at the back of the eye covered in millions of light-sensing cells. It works like a screen that turns light into messages for the brain.
asks: What is at the back of the eye?

facts: Light travels at about 300,000 kilometres per second, enough to circle the Earth about seven and a half times in one second.
The lens forms an upside-down image on the retina, which the brain interprets.

quiz.say: Why can you see a ball in a sunny garden?

options.show: Light bounces off it into your eyes
options.say: Light bounces off it into your eyes

options.show: Your eyes shine light on it
options.say: Your eyes shine light on it

quiz.why: Sunlight bounces off the ball and travels into your eyes.

wrong.1: Eyes do not give out light; they take it in.
wrong.2: A ball is not a light source; it only reflects light.

quiz.say: In a dim room, what happens to your pupils?
quiz.why: Pupils grow bigger to let in more light when it is dim.

wrong.1: Pupils get smaller in bright light, not dim light.
wrong.2: Pupils never disappear; they change size.
